consent.warningBody: This is a working demonstration rather than a finished product. It does what it says, and the format may still change - so keep anything you would be sorry to lose somewhere else as well.
consent.accept: I have read this and accept it
consent.proceedDisabled: Enter three Spanish words to continue
consent.remember: Don't show this again on this device

clause.gateway: The app itself is delivered through a public IPFS gateway, which sees that you loaded it. Your own Kubo node, or the IPFS Companion extension, fetches it from the network instead.
clause.relayOn: We run no server that keeps your list – but we do run a relay that introduces devices to each other. It may keep (pin) your list automatically so another device can collect it later, and it sees which addresses you open.
clause.networkOff: The network is off: no relay, no other devices. Nothing arrives and nothing leaves – except the archive, if you switch it on.
clause.listPasskey: The list behind the three Spanish words belongs to your passkey: only it writes, the same list on every device. Anyone with the words or the address gets the list.
clause.listOpen: The list behind the three Spanish words is open, as in the previous chapters: anyone with the words reads and writes.
clause.sealed: The entries are sealed with a key from your passkey: whoever gets the list cannot read it – the relay included. Only your passkey opens it, on every device. What such a key can and cannot do is the subject of the privacy01 chapter.
clause.notSealed: New entries are not encrypted: anyone with the three words reads them – including the relay that keeps the list. Entries sealed earlier stay readable with your passkey. The “Seal the list” box changes that; the privacy01 chapter shows how.
clause.sealingNeedsPasskey: Without a passkey the list is not encrypted: anyone with the three words reads everything – including the relay that keeps it. Sealing needs a passkey to supply the key; the privacy01 chapter shows how that works.
clause.identityPasskey: Your passkey identifies you to the other devices. It stays with your authenticator – in the device, on a security key, or in a password manager that may sync it between your devices. We never see it, and nobody else can write as you.
clause.identityAnonymous: You are using a random identity that exists only in this browser. Reload and it is gone, and nothing connects one visit to the next.
clause.identityAnonymousKept: You are using a random identity that exists only in this browser. It keeps it until you clear the site data; nothing links it to you.
clause.storageKept: This browser keeps the list, your language, the theme and the archive setting; with a passkey, its identifier too. Clear the site data and it is gone – except what the archive holds.
clause.storageMemory: Memory only: reload and the list in this browser starts empty. Language, theme and this decision stay.
clause.archiveOn: The archive is on: every change goes out shortly afterwards, sealed, to the chosen store. The store sees the account address, the channel, sizes and times, not the content; the balance of an address is publicly readable.
clause.archiveOnOwner: The archive is on: every change goes out shortly afterwards, sealed, to the chosen store. The store sees the account address, the channel, sizes and times, not the content. The owner account’s address and its grants are public on Aleph.
clause.archiveOff: The archive is off: nothing is kept outside this device until you switch it on in the “Archive” section.
clause.noTracking: No tracking cookies, no analytics. “Don’t show this again” remembers only that decision, on this device.

consent.identityExistingNone: Nothing is stored in this browser. We will ask your authenticator, which only works if the passkey carries its own details.

consent.mnemonicHelp: Share these three Spanish words to join the same public writable OrbitDB list. This is a share code, not a password or encryption key.
consent.mnemonicSrError: Enter exactly three valid Spanish words.
consent.identityCreateHint: Register a new WebAuthn passkey and derive your OrbitDB identity (DID) from it.
consent.identityCreateHintAnother: Register another WebAuthn passkey — a second identity alongside the one already on this device.
consent.identityAnonymousHint: Use a random per-browser identity, exactly like the previous chapter.

element.ok: A direct connection off this network looks possible.
element.unreliable: This network maps a new port per destination and offers no IPv6, so a direct connection usually works only to someone on this same network.
element.none: No path off this network was found. You can still connect to someone on this same network.
element.sameNetwork: Two devices on the same Wi-Fi connect regardless of any of this.
element.details: Show the addresses this check found
element.detailsHint: What a peer would be offered as a route to this device. Turn a VPN on or off and check again - if anything changed, it changed here.
element.detailsDecides: Only the "seen from outside" rows decide the verdict above. The rest are this device’s own addresses, which exist whether or not anything gets out.
element.candidateMdns: Addresses ending in .local are stand-ins the browser substitutes for this device’s own address, so a web page cannot read it. They are not a fault and they are not the VPN.
element.waysHeading: How the other device gets in
element.wayQr: By camera: you hold up a code, they scan it. Nothing leaves this network.
element.relayHint: For when the other device cannot scan your code - over a messenger, for instance. Off unless you ask for it.
element.relayChecking: Looking for a relay that answers…
element.relayNone: No relay answered. Scanning a code still works.
element.privacyHeading: What this means for your data
element.privacyEmpty: The choices above decide what goes here.
element.privacyAccept: I have read this and accept it
technical: A phone closes a waiting invite within seconds of you leaving the app. Only DuckDuckGo and Safari have been seen to hold one for about ten.
Chrome on Android reports no IPv6 where Firefox and DuckDuckGo on the same phone and the same Wi-Fi report one. A verdict describes this browser, not the network.
On mobile data, carrier NAT usually blocks a direct connection to anyone outside that network.
A VPN moves both ends somewhere else, which can fix a blocked network or break a working one.

consent.relayDiscovered: {count} relays found in the directory - the ones shipped with this app stayed silent.
consent.storageMemoryHint: Todos are stored in an OrbitDB database in memory – sealed, if you tick “Seal the list” below – and are gone on reload or exit.
consent.storagePersistentHint: I understand todos are stored in an OrbitDB database in the browser’s IndexedDB – sealed, if I tick “Seal the list” below – and persist between restarts.
consent.p2pOnHint: This browser connects to a relay and to other devices, and the list replicates between them.
consent.p2pOffHint: No relay, no other devices: the list does not replicate. The archive still talks to its store (upload, STORE, balance); nothing else leaves the browser. That is how to see what a restore alone gives back.

archive.title: Archive
archive.intro: Every change to the list goes out shortly after it is written, as a sealed increment, to a store outside this device. Nobody clicks and no other device has to be online; a wiped browser gets the list back with the same passkey.
archive.needsPasskey: The archive belongs to a passkey: it yields the account that keeps the increments and the key that seals them. Without one there is nothing here to archive.

storeHelp.aleph: No account and no key: the upload goes straight to Aleph's IPFS host, and a STORE order signed by the archive account keeps it, paid in credits on that account.
storeHelp.pinata: Needs the JWT of a Pinata API key. It is stored sealed with the backup key and used in this browser only.
storeHelp.lighthouse: Needs a Lighthouse API key; Lighthouse puts the file into a Filecoin deal. The driver has not been verified against a live account yet.
storeHelp.local: For trying it out: the increments stay in this browser's localStorage. That is no archive, but it shows what one would be.

archive.secretHelp: Sealed with the backup key from the passkey; it leaves the browser only as an Authorization header to the service.
archive.alephCredits: This account pays. Put credits on it (channel {channel}):
archive.none: The store holds nothing for this account.
archive.prfUnavailable: This authenticator gives no PRF output; no account and no key could be derived from it.
archive.prompts: One touch of the passkey per session: it yields the identity and the archive keys together. The keys stay in memory until the tab closes.
archive.creditsMeasured: measured: {hourly} credits an hour for {mib} MiB
archive.creditsEstimated: estimated from what was kept so far, 54 credits per MiB and day
archive.lockedHint: New browser, same passkey? “Restore from the archive” unlocks, finds the increments and brings the list back, with one touch of the passkey unless the start already had it.

progress.keeping: Asking the store to keep it …

archive.restoredOpened: The archive held a list other than the open one; it was opened under its own address and is now the open list:
archive.restoredCopied: {count} entries taken over from an earlier list; they are now written by this identity.
archive.memoryHint: Storage mode “in memory only”: the browser does not remember the archive’s setting or its numbering; after a reload the archive has to be switched on again, and the numbering comes back from the store.

deleteConfirm.aleph: Every increment this account keeps on the channel is forgotten on Aleph (a FORGET signed by the archive account). The files leave the nodes and stop costing credits. This cannot be undone.
deleteConfirm.pinata: Every increment of this archive is deleted at Pinata. This cannot be undone.
deleteConfirm.lighthouse: Every increment of this archive is deleted at Lighthouse. This cannot be undone.
deleteConfirm.local: Every increment in this browser is deleted.

archive.deleteNote: The list itself stays. The watcher starts over afterwards: the next increment carries the whole list again.
archive.alephCreditsOwner: The owner account pays. Put credits on it (channel {channel}):

payer.title: Who pays?
payer.info: Advantages and disadvantages of the two choices
payer.self: This archive account pays for itself
payer.selfShort: The key from the passkey is also the account holding the credits. Nothing to set up.
payer.owner: An owner account outside the browser pays
payer.ownerShort: The passkey key only signs; an account that never enters the browser is checked and billed. One command by the owner, once.
payer.selfPro1: Works at once: put credits on the address shown here, done.
payer.selfPro2: One key for everything, including deleting the archive from here.
payer.selfPro3: Nothing outside the browser: no CLI, no wallet, no second account.
payer.selfCon1: The key is in this tab. A bad dependency or an injected script can take it and spend the credits.
payer.selfCon2: Whoever has the key can forget the whole archive.
payer.selfCon3: Credits on it are probably movable by whoever has the key — keep the amount small.
payer.ownerPro1: A leaked browser key can only add storage on this channel. It cannot forget, and holds no credits.
payer.ownerPro2: One account can pay for several passkeys and devices, each granted and revoked on its own.
payer.ownerPro3: Revoking is one command by the owner; the archive stays.
payer.ownerCon1: One step outside the browser: the owner runs an `aleph` CLI command, once per key.
payer.ownerCon2: The owner account needs credits (and a payment credit) before the first STORE goes through.
payer.ownerCon3: Deleting from here needs a FORGET grant too, which gives a leaked key that power back; otherwise the owner deletes from outside.
payer.verdict: For a try-out, the first. For anything worth keeping, the second — the key that pays should not live where scripts run.
payer.forget: Also ask the owner for FORGET, so the archive can be deleted from here (a leaked key could then delete it too).
payer.granted: Grant in place: this key may STORE on the channel for the owner.
payer.grantedWithForget: Grant in place: this key may STORE and FORGET on the channel for the owner.
payer.notGranted: No grant yet: the owner has not authorized this key. Run the first command below, then check again.
payer.commandsHelp: Run where the owner’s key lives, with the owner as the active account (`aleph account use <name>`, aleph CLI 0.20.0). The list is the owner’s complete list of grants: others stay as they are, this key’s entry is set. Nothing here holds the owner’s key.

command.revoke: Revoke this key (the complete list without it)

payer.forgetNotGranted: The owner did not grant FORGET to this key, so the archive cannot be deleted from here. The owner deletes it with this command, or grants FORGET above and you try again.

prf.title: Now the keys from the passkey
prf.why: Your passkey gives the app a secret. It becomes the archive account and the key that seals the increments — and, for a new passkey, the key your entries are signed with. None of it is stored.

proof.title: Last: your signature
proof.why: Your passkey signs once that this identity's entries are yours. The browser keeps that signature; the next start does not ask again.

passkeySteps.notALoop: Each prompt has its own purpose; it is not a repeat. With a security key: touch it and, if asked, enter the PIN.
passkeySteps.restoreTouch: Passkey prompt 2 of {of}: a second signature your identity is computed from. Not a repeat.

sealList.title: Encryption
sealList.label: Seal the list
sealList.hint: Entries leave this browser only encrypted, with a key from your passkey. Every device with the same passkey reads them; the relay, and anyone with the three words, does not. More in the privacy01 chapter.
sealList.needsPasskey: Needs a passkey: it supplies the key. Without one the list stays open.
sealList.noPrf: The list could not be sealed: this authenticator gives no PRF output to make a key from. It is open, as the notice without the box says.

todo.sealedHidden: {count} entries are sealed and cannot be read without the key. Tick “Seal the list” at the next start, or switch the archive on, and the passkey supplies it.
